utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, this Wednesday. I'd first like to greet Mr. Petkovic, the other accused, the Defence, representatives of the OTP, my colleagues, and everyone else assisting us. The Chamber has two oral decisions it would like to render. Oral decision on the Petkovic Defence's request and the Prosecution's request to have additional time for the cross-examination of the witness Miroslav Desnica. In a request dated the 4th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence requested to be granted 15 minutes to conduct its cross-examination of the witness Miroslav Desnica, who will be appearing pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules, scheduled for the 2nd of March, 2010. This hearing is scheduled for the 2nd of March, 2010. The Coric Defence responded to the request on the 15th of February, 2010. The Chamber granted the Petkovic Defence leave to reply in an oral decision of the 16th of February. This response was filed on the 17th of February, 2010. In addition, in a request dated the 1st of February, 2010, the Prosecution requested to be granted one hour to examine the witness Miroslav Desnica. The Coric and Praljak Defence responded to the request on the 4th of February, 2010. The Prosecution asked leave -- requested leave to respond and filed its response on the 4th of February, 2010. The witness Miroslav Desnica, called by the Coric Defence, is to appear pursuant to 92 ter of the Rules on the 2nd of March, 2010. The Coric Defence informed the Chamber and the parties of its intention of conducting an examination-in-chief, the length of which would be 30 minutes. In view of the submissions filed by the parties, the Chamber hereby grants the Petkovic Defence's request to have 15 additional minutes for its cross-examination, to the extent that this request is not a disproportionate one and is in accordance with the practice of the Chamber with regard to allocating time for the cross-examination of a witness who is appearing pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Chamber hereby decides, for the very same reasons, to grant the Prosecution request and to grant it one hour for the conduct of its cross-examination. The Prlic Defence, the Stojic, Praljak, and Pusic Defence have not filed any requests in particular, but will have 30 minutes at their disposal which are to be divided amongst themselves in case they should wish to conduct their cross-examination. Second oral decision concerning Witness Andabak. Witness Janko Andabak, called by the Coric Defence, is to appear as a viva voce witness from the 2nd to the 4th of March, 2010. The Coric Defence has informed the Chamber and the parties of its intention to use two hours for the examination-in-chief of this witness and for any re-examination they might wish to conduct. In a request dated the 1st of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence requested leave to be granted an hour, which means that they would be granted 45 additional minutes in relation to the time they would allocated in accordance with Guide-line 5. They have requested this additional time for the examination of the witness Andabak. The Coric Defence responded on the 5th of February, 2010, to this request. The Chamber authorised the Petkovic Defence to file a response, which was done on the 12th of February, 2010. Then on the 2nd of February, 2010, the Praljak Defence filed a request and asked the Chamber for 20 additional minutes to conduct its cross-examination of this witness. And, finally, in a brief of the 10th of February, 2010, the Stojic Defence requested that the Chamber grant it 20 additional minutes to conduct its cross-examination of the witness. In addition, it requested that this additional time be allocated to the total time granted to it by the Chamber -- be deducted from the total time. Concerning the 65 ter summary of the witness Andabak, the Chamber believes that the requests for additional time filed by the Praljak Defence and the Stojic Defence have a good basis and are not disproportionate. The Chamber hereby decides that they be, therefore, granted 20 additional minutes for each team in order to cross-examine the witness. The Chamber also takes notes of the Stojic Defence request to have the additional time of 20 minutes added to its total time. As far as the Petkovic Defence team is concerned, the Chamber believes that an hour for its cross-examination is disproportionate, given the elements in the 65 ter summary for the witness Janko Andabak. The Chamber believes that 20 additional minutes is sufficient for counsel to protect its client's interests. As a result, time will be allocated as follows: The Coric Defence will have two hours for its examination-in-chief and for re-examination, if any. The Stojic Defence, the Praljak and Petkovic Defence, will have 32 minutes respectively for their cross-examination. Given that there are no particular requests from the Prlic and Pusic Defence teams, they will have 12 minutes respectively for any cross-examination they may have. And, finally, the Prosecution will have, pursuant to Guide-line 5, two hours for its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, with regard to the questions I will be putting to you concerning the list of exhibits dealt with on the first day and given the time taken yesterday that was spent on clarifying the oral decision that was handed down, in light of all those elements, I'll put questions to you with regard to two elements, the video of the bridge and I'll put questions to you on the document on a meeting that was held in Zagreb. Then I will put questions to you on the basis of documents from your own Defence team and will only be referring to 4D documents. That means to your documents. I will then conclude today. That is my intention. I won't be putting any questions to you tomorrow. Tomorrow, the D1 Defence team will conduct its cross-examination. Mr. Registrar, let's now see the video on the Old Bridge. Please view it carefully, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop there. General Petkovic, I've seen this video ten times, at least. As I did, you must have come to the conclusion that shots were fired. You can see the bridge being hit, and you can see that when the shell -- or when a shell hits the bridge, there's a sort of red bubble -- red effect that is produced, a red ball. Whereas you were in the JNA, in the unit that had artillery and missiles, shells, at one point in time, perhaps you could tell me what this red ball is when the shell hits the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when any shell hits a target, the red ball means that there was an explosion, because the explosive in the shell is being activated at the point of impact. So it's a red ball effect, which means, as I said, that the explosive in the shell has been activated, and it's when the detonator sets off the explosion and the fill. So if you were to set alight an explosive yourself, when it explodes you have this red ball flash effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's a very precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but it would be maybe useful to have the number of that video in the transcript. I think you mentioned it, but it was not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll have a number. It's Exhibit IC00574. General Petkovic, one can also see the third hit -- when the third shell hits the bridge, the red ball is on the other side of the bridge. How do you explain this? If you like, we can have a look at the video one more time. Would you like us to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no need. I've seen it. The red ball or red ball effect is the tracer that you can see, so it's a projectile that was fired from the opposite side of the bridge, so not from the southern side. It came somewhere from the north, that is to say, from the other side of the bridge. If we divide it into north and south, it came from the south [as interpreted] side, which means that there was something else which fired this one or more projectiles targeting the bridge, but from the opposite side of the bridge, from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Listen to me carefully now, General Petkovic. On the other side, when it comes from the north, who was present on the other side in the north? Who could have fired on the bridge from that side?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question now is of locality, location. The Neretva River, the bridge, north towards Tito's Bridge and that whole area were held by the BH Army forces. So from the bridge, the Old Bridge itself, right up until I think it was called Tito's Bridge and the barracks, that was held by -- well, along the Neretva River on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the importance of what you have just said, namely, that -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry to interrupt, but I think that the transcript, on lines from 12 to 18, does not really reflect what the witness said. The witness explicitly mentioned projectile coming from the north side. It is -- I don't think it is reflected here. I would kindly ask the Court to repeat this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the French interpretation, my understanding was that the projectile came from the north. I'll put my question to you again, because it's important in the video we saw. But before I put the question again, I will first ask the Registrar to show it again so that everyone can see this very clearly and so that the Prosecution can see this very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. We have just seen a shell that hit the bridge on the other side, and we saw a tyre fall on the other side of the bridge. General Petkovic, the shell that we have all just seen came from which direction?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that shell came from the north, from the northern side of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question: Which forces were present to the north of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north of the bridge, including both banks of the Neretva River, right up to Tito's Bridge, roughly, or even more northerly, the area of South Camp and Rastan, this area of Rastan was held by the BH Army, that area. So both sides of the Neretva, including North Camp, the area of North Camp. That's where members of the BH Army were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but let's clear something up, an imprecision. The general, first of all, said "South Camp and Rastani," and then later he said "North Camp." So just to avoid misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, that is North Camp. Yes, South Camp is elsewhere. So we're dealing with North Camp, and the BH Army took control of North Camp in June, which means that this entire area from north camp was held by the BH army right up to the Old Bridge, and further on along the Neretva River. But from the bridge to the north, that's North Camp and the entire area up to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to the last document, P07475. You must have it. It's the record of the meeting that was held on the 4th of January, 1994, in the Presidential Palace from 10.50 to 11.40. It's necessary to be extremely precise. And this meeting was attended by Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Susak, and Mr. Bobetko. General Petkovic, have you had the time to read this document, have a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have looked through this document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the Registrar put page 12 of the English version on the screen, and the identical page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I be allowed to say something about this document, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead. I have page 12 in your version. What did you want to say, General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you would be asking me first how this meeting came about in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This meeting -- or, rather, this is a record of the meeting. It's a Prosecution exhibit, as you are well aware. The presidential transcripts have been translated by using a recording that we don't have, we no longer have. The Judges never had it. We have an English version and a B/C/S version of these transcripts, so that's the document. This is not the first transcript, because a number of them have been admitted. Are there any comments you would like to make about this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, what I want to say is this: This conversation took place after Geneva on the 21st, and then on the 22nd and 23rd of December, 1993, in Brussels a meeting was held linked to an agreement about a union of three republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at which a framework was set. And according to that, 33 per cent would have been Muslims, 17.5 would have been the Croats, and 49.2 per cent would have been given to the Serbs. Now, this meeting on the 4th of January, 1994, between Tudjman, Susak and Bobetko, was prompted by that situation and what had happened prior to that in Brussels. So it is discussions about an international plan for the setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which defined the size of the territory, but also essentially -- if you look at the draft plan, it actually defines the different areas and regions that had previously been defined by the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. So there were certain deviations to that plan, where he accepted a part occupied by the army, and he added another part, if I can put it this way, to the Muslim side, because the HVO -- where the HVO had previously had control, which was the whole of Stolac municipality and a large portion of the Neretva River Valley, and so that's what they were discussing here in Zagreb at this meeting. Similarly, in the document we also see mention of the request to come out to the sea, to the coast, an exit to the sea. And on the basis of that, the Republic of Croatia and the leadership of Croatia, these three men, were discussing the fact that that part was threatened, and the border, meaning the border of the Republic of Croatia, with the intentions of these others to reach the sea; not to Neum, but another location, which was Klek. So that was what was discussed. And also another thing that was discussed was a very difficult situation in which the Croatian Defence Council found itself in the Central Bosnia area, and the danger of Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and the other areas to be wiped out completely, as far as the Croatian Defence Council was concerned. That means that the BH Army should take control of that area, too, and in that way the Croatian Defence Council and the Croats, themselves, quite simply wouldn't have 17 and a half per cent, they wouldn't even have 5 per cent. And the South Mostar area was questionable, too, because you had 100.000 BH Army forces joining up, and from Central Bosnia they could be deployed along the Neretva River towards the Republic of Croatia in their intention to reach the coast, to reach the sea, have an outlet to the sea. So that is the substance of these talks, and they were looking into ways and means of dealing with the situation, what they could advise the Croatian leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what they should tell them to do, and what would be the best option given the circumstances. And here we see that there are three options, three variants, put on the table, and then the worst-case scenario was if they jeopardise the Croatian borders down south, then Croatia will respond openly and actively and stop that kind of breakthrough. And then they looked into this northern part in relation to the area that should be the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which is the area of Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and so forth, and how to assist the Croats and the HVO in that part to prevent it falling into the hands of the BH Army, because it was under siege and that's where the most -- the heaviest fighting took place, including the beginning of 1994, when the fighting was fiercest. So it was in that context that the situation in the area was being reviewed. So that, in my opinion, was the substance of the talks and negotiations held, which is evidenced in this transcript between these three individuals. And now we can go on to other questions, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have given us the background to this document, so I can focus on the questions that I have in mind. You have page 12 on the screen, and Bobetko says the following: "I have contacts with Petkovic. He was away, and I told him that there has to be a person responsible within the Command. That's the very principle of war-making. Orders are given to those capable of carrying them out, and they have to be consolidated within the Command. One may be absent, but not all of them, day and night." When I read this sentence, my impression was that General Bobetko had difficulty in reaching you, and apparently he was not the only one. How do you explain that it was hardly ever possible to get in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the period around the new year, when I had some serious health problems. I had to go -- I don't know how you call it. We called it "hot shots." These were cocktail shots of various vitamins, B-6, B-12, for people with problems with their spine, and I had to have those shots daily. And I was keeping my back warm, I had massage and what is known as galvanisation of both shoulders, so over a period of some ten days, as long as this treatment lasted, I was absent from my command post. And General Bobetko had probably tried to reach me during that period, and he failed to reach me. That is the only problem. Otherwise, it was normal, if General Roso was absent, I would be at the command post or nearby. The only problem was that he called me and he couldn't reach me because I was absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Registrar to show us page 10 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I'm reading the English text of this transcript now. Could we go back to page 12, please. And I can see that it wasn't correctly translated. The word "the same" is missing. "I have contacts with Petkovic. He was also away now, and I told him ...," et cetera. The word "also" is missing, which significantly changes the meaning. In the Croatian text, it is clear that Bobetko tried to reach General Roso, but that he also tried to reach Petkovic and he couldn't find him either. So from the English translation, that doesn't emerge and it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10, please. Page 10, please. That's it. General Petkovic, you see, in the middle of page 10, there's

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK WHO SAYS
utterances.text: "We are having dinner with Galbraith on Wednesday." But just before that, there's Mr. Tudjman, who says the following, and I quote: "Who told him to ask for a visa for him to be able to travel, so that we may cleanse our image in the eyes of the world, though I keep repeating, and I will continue repeating, and again in this letter to Izetbegovic, that Boban is a product of the Serb aggression." And Tudjman then, after Susak's comment, says the following: "Then you repeat this directly, Boban might be held partly politically responsible, and here is what happened to him. They knocked the bridge down, but that is the war, and he emerged as part of the resistance to the Serb aggression, and therefore we wished him -- to have him so as to be able to reach an agreement with the Muslims." So have you seen this sentence where Tudjman talks about Boban and says that Boban is a product of the Serb aggression? What would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, President Tudjman is trying to say that had it not been for the Serb aggression, Mate Boban would certainly not be in the post he was. He was the organiser of the rallying of the Croats and the organiser of the resistance against the Serb aggression, the aggression in April 1992 and onwards. So here Galbraith and many others are bringing pressure to bear on President Tudjman, saying that Mate Boban's time is over and that certain measures should be taken for Mate Boban to leave that position and for someone else to be found to replace him. And towards the end, President Tudjman says, We want him to be able to reach an agreement with the Muslims. What he means is, We want to remove Mate Boban or for him to leave so that an agreement could be reached with the Muslims, if Mate Boban is the one who is to blame. Therefore, after this meeting, shortly after this meeting, at the beginning of February Mate Boban will officially be removed from his position and replaced by someone else. So these reflections were under pressure of Galbraith, who is asking for Mr. Boban to withdraw and for someone else to be found for this position. That is the substance of this discussion between them. And this, in fact, happened. I don't remember the exact date when Mr. Boban left and Zubak came in his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two other questions with this document. Page 14, please. I wish to see page 14 in the English and B/C/S version on the screen, please. Here we have it. Third line, I'm going to read, and then you're going to tell me what you think. Line 3: "I said to Petkovic today," and this is Bobetko speaking, "that now, today, a new mobilisation should commence, and I ordered that this 8th Light holding positions at Ogulin as a reserve be transferred down there for manoeuvre or that we go up there towards this part in the direction of Travnik." General Petkovic, that is what Bobetko is saying. And when I read this, I could come to the following conclusion, for as you know, the Rules make it my obligation, as well as the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, to establish the truth. That is my moral obligation that is imposed upon me. And when I read this text, I could conclude that General Bobetko is calling on you and asking you for a new mobilisation, and I seem to understand that the 8th Light is holding positions at Ogulin and there appears to be the possibility of moving them towards Travnik. Does the 8th Light come from the Croatian Army? If so, that means that you are associated with a movement of troops involving the Croatian Army. I may be wrong. What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if General Bobetko says, I told Petkovic today, and we saw that he couldn't find Petkovic, so there's some contradiction here. Furthermore, I will say, without insulting General Bobetko, as he's an elderly gentleman, that this is a nice story that he served on President Tudjman. The 8th Light Brigade never came to Vakuf, nor was that brigade of the Croatian Army moved towards Gornji Vakuf. And I can prove this by showing a document. When there is reference to the forces, you will not be able to find the 8th Light Brigade anywhere. I'm sorry I have to say this here, but these are stories in the presence of President Tudjman, and that they are unfounded. And I repeat, the 8th Light Brigade never, never came to the territory of Gornji Vakuf, and I will refer to a document where you will see not that there is no 8th Light Brigade, there's none at all. Now, why such a story is served on President Tudjman, I wasn't present at the meeting, so I couldn't have -- I couldn't say, You can't say these things, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I take note that for you, the 8th Light Brigade was not, as one might conclude from the document, in Travnik, and it was not present in the Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that this, a fable, a story, for President Tudjman. I take note of this. I come to my last question on this document. Page 19, please. It will be a purely technical question regarding aerosol bombs. We have page 19. It's Bobetko who's speaking. He says the following: "One cluster bomb was fished out from the seas at Lopud. It came down the Neretva River. We have been investigating who was the person who let it float down the river. It had a 36-hour Swiss mechanism. We gave them this bomb, but we don't know where it came from. Did they capture it, or did someone throw it into the water?" For me, this is absolutely unclear. This cluster bomb, was it given to the HVO or the Croat Army? And where is Lopud; is it in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Lopud is a small island close to Dubrovnik in the south of Croatia. This is not a cluster bomb. It is an anti-navy bomb, a floating bomb or a diving one that is put into the sea and waits for an enemy ship to come across it. Those are bombs that are dropped into the sea. I don't know how it came to the Neretva River. The Croatian Army -- or, rather, the JNA did not leave such bombs. Whether, upon leaving the port of Ploce, the JNA may have left some of those bombs in front of the port of Ploce, and they may have floated towards Dubrovnik, which is about 150 kilometres, the sea current may have carried it, and the former units for mine-laying of the JNA was based in Ploce. There was no base on the Neretva for such naval bombs to be found there. These are naval bombs whereby one prevents the possible movement of enemy vessels. They float in the sea and may be encountered by an enemy ship. And one knows what happens then. And one such bomb reached as far as Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this answer. General Petkovic, I'm going now to refer to all the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to ask two questions. One relates to what you have said a while ago. It is page 14, line 25, and the next line. You said: "... shortly after this meeting, at the beginning of February, Mate Boban will officially be removed from his position." And my question is: Who will remove him, or who did remove him, and how was that done?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Trechsel, in Livno, I think it was, a meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and all the other political factors of Herceg-Bosna attended a meeting, and they made the decision to relief Mate Boban of his duties. So it was in February. I don't know the exact date. I'm not sure. There was a session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and all other relevant political factors in Herceg-Bosna attended, and they decide to relieve Mate Boban of his duties. And Mr. Zubak was appointed in his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second question relates to the document we have just seen and to something Mr. Bobetko said just after the passage the President has quoted on page 14. He says, and I quote: "Secondly, we got some arms so that we can control the entire Neretva Valley north of the Neretva with two or three multiple rocket-launchers, thence this is what we can guarantee completely, that not a single bird would escape us." This looks as if General Bobetko were saying it is easy, with two or three multi-rocket-launchers, to control the access to the north from Mostar and lock in the Muslims of Eastern Mostar. I may misunderstood even this. I would like you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the answer, let me say that the text refers to the area north of the Neretva and not north of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just see which page this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's page 14 in the English version. Ms. Alaburic, could you explain? I was of the opinion that the Neretva was a river that came from the north to Mostar. And, of course, north-east of the Neretva was HVO territory, but north-west, as I seem to remember, would have been the territory where the Defences always say it was no problem to get to and from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately I'm not an expert for the area. But the situation isn't that simple, because part of the Neretva Valley is completely in the Republic of Croatia. The continuation of the Neretva Valley is under the control of the Croatian forces on both sides of the river, on the left and the right side, and then to the north of Mostar, the right bank is under the Croatian forces and the left bank under the Muslim forces. And then the positions get mixed up and both have the left and right bank. It's not that easy. I just want to do say that Mostar, as a town, isn't mentioned at all. So I just want to avoid confusion about the territory concerned. If I was mistaken, could someone correct me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have confused me a bit, and that is your role. I don't really understand whether you want to interpret General Bobetko or whether you just want to say that his statement is equivocal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my role is to help you to fully understand the situation, at least to the extent that I can understand the situation, and I really would like you to take my efforts in that sense. I wanted to avoid any confusion, because you referred to the passage that starts with the words "Other," but then it was almost a quote when you mentioned the territory to the north of Mostar. All I wanted to say is that the words Bobetko used were "to the north of the Neretva."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Alaburic, if you have listened carefully, I have read exactly these words. Then I have asked Mr. Petkovic about what they actually mean, and I would like him to answer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Bobetko -- well, if we have a look at the bottom part, General Bobetko says that he will secure reserve forces. He mentions Marinovic and 700 men, and they would have fire support. And he says they can be on the one of the axis or second axis or third axis according to need. General Bobetko will bring into the territory of the lower part of the Neretva forces 700-men strong. They will be provided with fire support, and they will control any breakthrough to the south of Mostar towards the border with Croatia. So that's why these intervention forces were brought to the territory of the Valley of Neretva, but in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, or, rather, he planned to bring these forces in. I can't say whether that was done, but he's thinking of moving 700 men to the lower part of the Neretva, which is in the Republic of Croatia. He would reinforce them with two or three VBRs, and to the south of Mostar they can put up resistance if an attempt is made to break through to Croatia. That's what he had in mind, and that's what the reference to two or three VBRs means. And Gojko is supposed to bring in a group, too. So these are all forces that were to be used to secure Klek, Neum, Ploce, to secure these territories. And when he says "to the south," he means to the south of the Croatian border. The Neretva flows through Croatia, and to the north of it you have the area that is to the south of Mostar. So if you head south from Mostar in the direction of Croatia, he would be ready to intervene with those forces and to support them with the artillery that he had secured.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 13 and 12, the term "south" is used. The general said, when Bobetko says "to the north," he means to the north of the border, so it should say "north" and not "south."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bobetko was expecting the ABiH from the Dubrava Plateau to enter the territory of Croatia, and that is why he was planning to use reserve forces that he would deploy in the Metkovic, Ploce, Opuzen area, and in such a case he would prevent the breakthrough of Muslim forces from the plateau -- of the Dubrava Plateau. And he used two or three VBRs for this purpose, multiple rocket-launchers. We can see the mortars he has referred to, et cetera. So he's giving Nojko [phoen] support, fire support, and he won't allow the ABiH to enter the Republic of Croatia from Blagoje and the Dubrava Plateau. So that was his intention, and he formed these intervention forces for such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I was, indeed, misled, it seems, by the text, and you have set this clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I'm going to put some questions to you on the basis of documents. Before I do so: I carefully read the submissions filed by your counsel on the 15th of February, 2006. This is your pre-trial brief. I read through it. It consists of more than 35 pages. I read through it carefully in order to understand what the Petkovic Defence's view was. I also read with great interest the entire file provided to us by Ms. Alaburic with regard to the opening statement. I congratulate her, because it's very well drafted and composed. It was very easy for me to check up certain things. On that basis, I have selected a series of documents, and I will put some questions to you on the basis of those documents. The first one is 4D1700. It should be the first document in your binder. I'm waiting to see the document before I put the question to you, out of courtesy towards the other accused who don't have the binder. We have the text in B/C/S, and in English, too. As you can see, it is a document that was drafted by Colonel Blaskic. It's an order which you approved of, because we have that reference, "I approve." I'm interested in the first word, where Colonel Blaskic speaks about the area of Central Bosnia, and he says that the enemy has conducted offensive operations. To be very careful and to fully understand the idea of offensive and defensive operations, tell me, what does General Blaskic mean when he says that the ABiH is conducting offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ABiH wasn't conducting operations of any kind. The Army of Republika Srpska was. The entire front part refers to -- the entire first part refers to units from the Army of -- let me just check this. There are three and a half pages in the Croatian version where General Blaskic describes the intention of the Army of Republika Srpska. After taking Jajce, they arrived in Travnik, and they wanted to continue to take the entire area of Central Bosnia. So Blaskic is talking about potential offensives launched by the Army of Republika Srpska in the Central Bosnian area, which is being defended in a joint manner with the ABiH. So all these units which you see referred to on pages 1, 2, and 3 are units that belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska, units that were deployed in the vicinity of the central area of, let's say, the free Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Republika Srpska Army was conducting offensive operations. As far as you know, did the ABiH, in 1992 and 1993, conduct offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as this document is concerned, we will later see that Blaskic was planning to prevent an attack launched by the Serbian forces by acting in a joint manner with the ABiH. We're talking about the month of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at five -- let's have a look at page 10, please. I didn't have the intention of putting this question to you, but as your answer concerned the VRS, I want to go into the ABiH. So let's have a look at page 10. Bobovac -- 5.10 is the item. "The Bobovac Brigade," is what I'm interested in. You can see that the task is mentioned. A co-ordinated action is to be conducted together with the ABiH. Active operations are to be conducted. Does this mean that at the time the ABiH and the HVO conducted offensive operations against the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this item of the order, Blaskic issued such an order to his brigade. The brigade was to defend the area facing the VRS. The ABiH were in the vicinity, too. And he was requesting [realtime transcript read in error "requested"] that they not remain in the trenches, but that they also engage in certain actions and inflict losses on the VRS. And perhaps they would also manage to liberate part of the occupied territory. That's the terminology -- the JNA terminology that was used. Conduct active operations when you're engaged in defence. So the Bobovac Brigade and the unit from the ABiH, the Vares Brigade and the ABiH, jointly organised defence and prevented enemy forces from breaking through, enemy forces from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the time the HVO and the ABiH were acting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to intervene regarding the transcript. On line 18, the sentence is -- the response is recorded as "and he was requested." It is about Blaskic, "like somebody else requested." General Petkovic clearly said Blaskic requested. It's not that he was requested, but he requested orders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll conclude with this document. In your mind, is there a difference between an offensive action and an active action or active operation, or is it the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this entire order is an order for defence. It means that the forces are to defend the territory. That's the main task. But each unit is given the possibility of taking more active -- a more active stance with regard to the enemy, to take part of the territory, and to move the front-line. So this is a defensive order. It's not a -- this is a defensive order, not an offensive order. An offensive order would say which axis it should follow, what should be taken, how soon, and so on and so forth. So the title is "Order for Defence," but this defence can't be envisaged in a static manner. If there is an opportunity, one can take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Scott, if I may, until we have a page on the screen, but whatever. Your Honour, I did intervene, and it is again repeated, something which is not said. I kindly ask you to ask a direct question to the general, whether the text -- whether he said that Blaskic was requested or whether the testimony is that Blaskic requested the others. I mean, in spite of intervention, it is again the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Let me check something before I -- yes, Your Honour. If we could get a date for this document. As the Chamber knows well by now, dates are incredibly important, and we have no idea if this is 1991, 1992, 1994, or 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. No, excuse me, excuse me. Let's let the witness answer. We don't need Ms. Alaburic testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. General Petkovic, in your opinion, this order, what is the date of the order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drafted in March 1993. I can't tell you the exact date. It's not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To understand what you have been saying, to fully understand what you're saying, because it's not the first time we've heard this, when we have "Order" marked in a document, a defence order, order for defence, within the document there may be a reference made to active operations or to offensive operations, but they would come under the heading of defence, they would be labelled as "Defence." Is that how we are to understand this in military terms? I'm not a military man, so I would like you to clarify this for me.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when an order is issued for defence, an order like the one we have here, its main purpose is for defence, the Serbian forces mustn't break through the defence line. But Blaskic assigns or gives each brigade the possibility of taking action. If they have the opportunity, if they have the forces, then they can engage in active operations. So that means that they can go forward from this line. It wouldn't be significant breakthroughs. Perhaps it would involve an area of 300 or 500 metres. But when you speak about offensive operations, then what one has in mind is really an attack. So under defence, the JNA meant "defence," but also active operations, active operations which involved in smaller areas. It means you don't allow the enemy to attack you. Take action in the direction of the enemy, inflict losses, disrupt the enemy's deployment, and then your defence will be more secure. So the active operations within defence, but "offensive action" means that you plan to carry out an attack, you really plan to carry out an attack. And let me repeat Mr. Kovacic's comment. Blaskic, through his order, asked every brigade -- each and every brigade to be active along the lines it held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the counsel refrain from intervening - I would be extremely grateful - unless there is a monumental error in the transcript. If there's an error in the French version, I'm aware of it. So, General Petkovic, let us look at the document 4D410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have still a question on the previous document. As I don't have it before me, I cannot look for indicia myself. Mr. Petkovic, can you tell the Chamber, was this order actually issued, or is it an order that was prepared but did not eventually go to the subordinate units, as one often has?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, this order went down to every brigade, and it was on the basis of this order that every brigade had to draft its own order for further action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the document 4D410, which is a decree of law issued by Mr. Izetbegovic personally on the 6th of August, 1992. Look at Article 1. Mr. Izetbegovic says, in November 1992, that the armed forces of the republic comprise the ABiH and, according to my understanding, the HVO is a component of the army. How would you interpreter this article as it is worded and coming from Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic here was playing a game, himself, but we take it at face value here. What he said is that the armed forces of the republic were comprised of the army, the BH Army, so that was an armed force hereinafter called "the army." But then he went on to say that the a constituent part of the BH Army shall comprise the Croatian Defence Council. So that was how it was, as interpreted by Izetbegovic here. Somebody obviously prepared this document from his legal office. So the HVO was part of the BH Army, and the BH Army was part of the forces. So the logical conclusion is that the HVO was a component part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that for Mr. Izetbegovic, the HVO was a part of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You are confirming what is written in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not entirely correct, Your Honour. That's not what's written, because what's written is "such units which place themselves under the command of the BiH government." I don't think we can take one part of the sentence without taking the other part of the sentence. So he is not confirming what is written, because you have not read the entire sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, could you read, in your own language, Article 1? Read it slowly, please, so that the interpreters into English can translate it properly for Mr. Scott. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The armed forces of the republic are made up of the Army of the Republic (hereinafter the Army). "A constituent part of the army shall comprise --" or, rather, "the Croatian Defence Council shall constitute part of the army as well as other armed components which place themselves under the single command of the army. "During a state of war, in addition to the Army, the armed forces shall be comprised of the police, units providing physical security to enterprises and other legal entities, units of the Customs Service and other frontier organs which are subordinated to the single command of the armed forces which are re-subordinated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Article 1, as you have read it and as it has been interpreted into English and French, says that the HVO is a part of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the HVO is placed under the single command of the ABiH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. We were part of the BH Army, and thereby we were a component part of the armed forces, and we were under the single command of the BH Army or, rather, the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that supreme single command was the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the unified supreme command depended on the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have added this. We are now going to look at the next document, 4D433. It's a document. I wait for it to appear on the screen. There it is. It's a document of the 20th of January, 1993. The dates are important, as Mr. Scott and Mr. Stewart have reminded us on several occasions. We'll always need to indicate the date, and I'm trying to do that. This is a document that you sent to Mr. Sagolj in person in Konjic, and this document relates to the situation. And you're asking him to establish contact with the ABiH. Do you remember this document, and what was the purpose of your request addressed to Sagolj? What is the context of all this, bearing in mind there's reference also to Zuka's men?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the context of all this is the following: that in the Konjic area, there should be talks between the HVO commander and members of the BH Army, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to prevent any tensions in the area in Konjic municipality, because we're warning them that the Chetniks are also planning to enter Konjic and take control of it. So they have to discuss the situation, reach an agreement, and do away with any tension. And bear in mind that there was this threat from the Chetniks storming Konjic and taking control of it. Now, Juka is an additional piece of information here, something that we learnt about, that after the conflict with Juka and these others, that he fled to the area of Konjic. And to ensure peace in the area, I ask him to relocate Juka's men from the territory to prevent them from being a cause for tension between them and the BH Army and the HVO, because the army -- BH Army incarcerated Juka, whereas the others considered him a hero and celebrated him. So that was the problem -- and released him from prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the explanation for this text. As we are talking about January, all the more reason to look at a map. We are going to look at 4D560, which we're going to see on the screen now. Here we are. Let us turn it around. That's it. We see this map now, which is the situation as it was in January 1993. Your counsel has said that you, yourself, drew this map and painted the colours indicating the positions of the Serbs, the ABiH, and the HVO, and that is the precise situation as it was in 1993 that was to have been conveyed to those in Geneva. This is not the first time we are seeing this map. I have looked at it at great length from all possible angles. I would like you, in military terms, but quite quickly so that we don't spend hours on it, that you explain to me the military position of the HVO as we see it in blue. I note that in blue there are enclaves at Zepce, Vares, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and then the other part, Jablanica, Livno, Tomislavgrad. So I see the positions of the HVO, and I also see the VRS and the ABiH. Could you please explain for us, from your point of view, what was the military situation, and was it critical or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll start off with Vakuf in January 1993, and that is denoted as a place of conflict. There was, indeed, a conflict, and it was stopped by the end of the month. You saw my order from Geneva, and that's when the conflict in Vakuf municipality was halted. Now, what is important is the arrow between Busovaca and Fojnica, or, rather, Kiseljak. This arrow shows that from the 25th to the 29th of January, 1993, the BH Army cut across the Croatian enclaves which are in blue, it split it in two. So from that time on, we had a separate enclave in Fojnica, Kiseljak, and Kresevo, that was one, and can I add -- and the other enclave which was separated was Busovaca, Vitez, and part -- a part belonging to Zenica municipality, Novi Travnik and Travnik. So the Central Bosnian part, where the Croats were a compact entity, in January, that is to say, from the 25th to the 9th of January, the BH Army cut across this enclave, making two enclaves of the Croatian Defence Council, and they remained that way until after the Dayton Accords. May I have a pen so that I can write in "Enclave 1" and "Enclave 2"? [Marks] So this one enclave was split into two. We have one which was made up of Fojnica, Kiseljak and Kresevo, and number 2, the second enclave, made up of Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, and Novi Travnik municipalities. And this area here [marks] -- so there's no more blue in this area. This was the area controlled by the BH Army along a line from -- ranging from seven to ten kilometres, and so that was the separation line of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian people living there. And that's how the situation remained until after the Dayton Accords. The HVO was never able to establish contact after this so that people could go freely from Kiseljak to Busovaca, or vice versa. By this action, the BH Army scored a considerable advantage, because it separated the Croats in this area, and there was no possibility for Vitez, Busovaca, if the need arose, could help, militarily, Kiseljak, Fojnica, and Kresevo. Now, the other areas, Kakanj, Vares, and so on, stayed the same as they had been previously. They were no longer able to communicate with any Croat -- Croatian enclave. Everybody was cut off in his own region. And there's another piece of information that I failed to tell you for the Konjic area. The arrow there indicates the arrival of units who were not from Konjic proper. They were the Black Swans, and we mentioned Zuka's men previously, part of the Lasta or Swallows, part of the Special Police of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were pulling out of Sarajevo and coming into the Konjic area, and there was some other smaller units as well which were infiltrating into Konjic. And that is why I am cautioning my commander to talk to the BH Army so that the influx of these forces should not lead to greater tension in Fojnica municipality and Konjic, Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you have marked this map, yourself, let us give an IC number to this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked portion of document 4D00560 shall be given Exhibit number IC01181. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After the break, we will see document 4D100. So the Registrar can prepare the document. That will be the next document after the break of 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the next document, which I think is already on the screen, 4D100. Here we are. It's an interview that you gave on the 16th of February, 1993. The date is February, and you're answering questions put by the reporter. First of all, will you please look at the second paragraph, when the reporter says: "Mr. Petkovic, it is impossible to find you at HVO headquarters in Mostar." So everyone is looking for you, and they can't find you, including reporters. And then you answer: "I am in the field most of the time ..." What would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the time of active negotiations in Geneva, and it was the duty, after the first half of the meeting, for me to meet with my commanders with respect to the orders issued and the documentation. I had to personally go and take a look at it, examine it, and then briefly to convey what had happened in those first days of negotiations and talks, those that I was able to reach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to look at page 3 in the English version. In my document, there are no page numbers, but it is a question being put in connection with Halilovic regarding extremist Muslims. There's no page number. Here we are. We see it, the box, in English, "10.000 Muslim extremists." And the Registrar is doing a miracle, and I'm sure he's going to be able to find the text in your own language. General Petkovic, the reporter is asking you whether Sefer Halilovic is behind the Muslim extremists who are provoking clashes, and you answer at length. We are not in the tu quoque, we are in a military context where we have belligerence, the HVO and the ABiH, and in the ABiH there are certain individuals. So the question put to you by the reporter is being answered by you. Would you, today, give the same answer as you did then?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I would give the same answer. The journalist asked the question, and the journalist said that it was 10.000 extremists. But I said that it was impossible to have 10.000 extremists, that it was a regular army, and that the situation we looked at a moment ago on the map, when Busovaca was cut off from Kiseljak, that's the area it applied to where the BH Army attacked the Croatian Defence Council, separated the two enclaves, Busovaca from Kiseljak, creating two enclaves. And that's what my answer was. I claim that it was not 10.000 extremists, but that it was 10.000 regular soldiers who had been given the assignment to attack the HVO and cut across Busovaca and Kiseljak, and they succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to look at the last page of the interview, when the journalist asks you a question about Mladic and Karadzic. Last page, please. Here it is. I have it in the English version. The journalist speaks about the negotiations in Geneva and asks you whether you had any meetings or contacts with the criminals Mladic and Karadzic. When the journalist qualifies them as criminals, what was your reply to the journalist's question?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my reply to the journalist was this: that according to the Geneva negotiations -- well, at the Geneva negotiations there were no bilateral talks; that I worked in the military -- well, we all worked in plenary sessions, sitting down at the same table, the Muslims, the Croats, the Serbs, and Mr. Satish Nambiar with his team, who conducted the negotiations and talks. And the journalist was interested in whether during our talks we had individual one-on-one talks. But I said, no, we didn't, that we all discussed matters together sitting down at a single negotiating table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to assess the weight to be attached to the question and the reply, this interview was in a publication issued in Zagreb, was it, in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Where was this magazine or newspaper published?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the Zagreb "Vecernji List" paper, but this edition was the edition for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the "Vecernji List" had a publication for Croatia and an additional publication which was intended for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that newspaper. Is it a totally independent newspaper in relation to the authorities of Croatia, or was it under the control of Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was an independent paper, but I don't know whether they were within the RPH. But as a newspaper, yes, it was independent with respect to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that the journalist was quite free to ask you any questions he wanted, and quite independent in doing so?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This journalist originated from Herzegovina, and he was a correspondent of the "Vecernji List," working for the "Vecernji List," but covering Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I have two questions with regard to this document. The first question is: Did you have a chance to re-read the text before it was published?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the text that figures in the box, you say, on the ABiH, that they are digging bunkers in every village. Digging bunkers, according to you, is it an activity which points to attack, rather, or rather to defence, or neither?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I toured the area, I was surprised why they were digging bunkers around each village. Well, the army didn't have any work to do, so to engage them they said, Let's dig the bunkers. So I think that's the simplest answer why bunkers were being built, and probably some other plans too. Every village wanted to protect itself because it didn't know who was going to attack it from where. So there was general hysteria in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two following documents relate to Safet Cibo, 4D450 and 4D452. 4D452. You have the text in your own language. This is 450. SDA. Mr. Cibo is going to be appointed at the same time by Halilovic and by the SDA, which is a political party, as a member of the regional committee for Herzegovina, and also he's going to be appointed by Halilovic for a military post 3252. And this is to show what? What did you wish to demonstrate with this type of document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at the previous document, we'll see that he was appointed to the post of president of the Wartime Presidency of Konjic municipality and Jablanica, so that was the post he occupied. Now, with this document, Sefer Halilovic is putting him at a high place in the Command of the 4th Corps of the BH Army. That is to say, he was given a military function as well. And then the regional board of the party, incorporating Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, is co-opting him into the party, so that to all intents and purposes he held all functions -- military and political functions in the area. And I think that that was the only man in Bosnia-Herzegovina who had functions of this type. And this "3252" is the VES from the JNA which denotes that he was a physician, a doctor, according to military terminology. Those are the figures and code for physicians, although he was assistant for morale and religious affairs. And he might have also been a commander, too, a shadow commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that Mr. Cibo had a double hat, a military one and a political one, at the same time. To the best of your knowledge, within the HVO were there people who also wore such two hats, who were at the same time military figures and politicians, like Cibo?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not. In the HVO, somebody could have a rank, could hold a rank, but need not have had a military function, because politicians could have been rewarded for their acts by some rank. But that they had a political function in the army, I don't know of any such case in the HVO. He is also the representative of executive power and authority here, which is his third function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll have a look at the document from the 4th Corps, 4D438. There it is. In the B/C/S version, it's not very legible. The English version is a lot more legible. It has to do with the 4th Corps. The date is the 24th of March, 1993. We learn that 150 members of the HVO were captured, that a town is blocked, that life in the town is paralysed, and that they're continuing with arrests. In your opinion, what does this document mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 23rd of March was when the all-out attack of the ABiH started from the area of Konjic. It was launched against two battalions of the HVO in the municipality of Konjic, and this report from the commander, Commander Cerovac, is a report on what he and his brigade had managed to achieve up until then. And he's reporting to his superior command, his 4th Corps, about that. So this is a report on his offensive operations against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have a look at 4D125, which is a document that you signed together with Mr. Pasalic, which is why it is a document of interest, in relation to the other documents that we have already seen that concerned the army and whether it was a joint army or not. There is your signature, and there is also Mr. Pasalic's signature on the document. The heading of the document is "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then it says "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council." And it also says "The HVO" and "The 4th Corps Command." So that is what a reasonable Judge can read in this document. If I have a look at item number 1, there is a joint order, HVO and BH Army order, and it says that all action should immediately cease. General Petkovic, it's a Defence document, not a Prosecution document. It was found in the archives of Croatia. What is the meaning of this document, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was drafted after eight or ten hours of combat in Konjic on that day. In the afternoon, I called Mr. Pasalic and asked him about what was going on in the territory of Konjic. I asked him whether we could put an end to that, whether he had the will and the force to put an end to the fighting in Konjic. He responded to my request. He came to the Main Staff to see me -- to the headquarters. We drafted this joint order and sent it to Konjic, to the HVO and to the ABiH, and we asked them to do what is stated here in this order. But we also told them that the situation in the battle-field of the Tuzla battle-field was difficult. It's in the direction of Zepa, Srebrenica, and so on. We asked them to put an end to the fighting, because at that point in time -- well, a witness appeared, Mr. Mlakar [phoen] here. He had received equipment from the HVO and was waiting for an end to the combat so that he could move the equipment to Tuzla through Jablanica and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, this document bears a number that you gave it and that he gave it. Does this number, 01/508/93 mean that this document emanates from you, who was number 1 in the HVO staff? So it's the 508th document emanating from 01; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's 01-508 is a number from my protocol, and to the right you have the number from the 4th Corps protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You anticipated my following question. To the right, apparently, Mr. Pasalic wrote down the number "01 ," that means him as commander of the 4th Corps, "2.192," so he must work more than you, four times more than you, because there are 2.192 documents, whereas you only had 508 documents. Apparently, he was a lot more active than you were. And then we have "/93." What did he do? How is it that he provided this number? That doesn't have a seal or stamp, as you can see, and he was in your office. Did he phone his office to be provided with this number? How was this done, if you can remember? I can't answer such questions because my memory doesn't allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was drafted in my office. He phoned his corps command and asked which the following number was. They told him what it was, and he then made a note of this number on the document. The official in charge of protocol told him that the following number was 2192, so he made a note of the number, "01-2192," and that's how it was sent later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me the exact date -- well, in fact, it says the 23rd of March, 1993. Is that correct? Because in the English version, there is no date, but in the B/C/S version there is a date. You see, it's always necessary to have a look at a document in the original version. You can see that the English translation doesn't bear the date.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 23rd of March is the date in the original signed by Pasalic and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, General Petkovic, listen to me carefully. If -- as a Judge reads who this document, who sees that it refers to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it refers to the HVO and to the 4th Corps, who sees that a joint order is being drafted, if I read this, as such a Judge, can I draw the conclusion that on a given date, the 23rd of March, 1993, the HVO and the ABiH were part of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or if I drew such a conclusion, would that conclusion be erroneous?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is correct. We were members of the very same army, and that's why we issued an identical order, the same type of order. And let me add, under item 1 we say that we don't want to disrupt the joint combat of the HVO and the ABiH, so there is joint combat. We have a common enemy, and it's necessary to put an end to the situation that had developed between the HVO and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at 4D469. The date is the 30th of March. I'm following the chronology. Sometimes I move from one subject to another, but I'm doing it in chronological order. It's a report from the HVO Crime Department. Ivica Kraljevic signed the document. I won't deal with the substance of the document, but at the time were you aware of the fact that there was a crime department?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A crime department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what was its main role? What was its main task?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a crime department within the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the military police. This department that was in charge of investigations, was it responsible, as far as you know, to investigate crimes committed by HVO soldiers, or was it only responsible for investigating crimes committed by members of the ABiH, ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, they investigated each and every case that occurred in the territory, not only crimes. There were also cases of theft. There was fighting. Certain units would flee. There were accidents, and HVO soldiers guilty of murder. So they investigated all these matters. They weren't only concerned with crimes, as you say. Their scope of activity was very broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a look at a map that you drafted in April, 4D561, because now we're dealing with the month of April. We saw the January map a while ago, and now we have a map relating to April. With regard to January -- well, now it's April. And with regard to January, what sort of significant changes occurred, in military terms, in the area that we can see in the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, I'll start again and check whether we are receiving interpretation. Yes, there is interpretation into English. I'll check to see whether I can hear the B/C/S. Yes, I do, on channel 6. General Petkovic, it's a map dated March-April 1993. A while ago, we saw the map from January. In what way had the military situation changed in relation to the January map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the situation changed in the following manner: Under 1, in the territory of the municipality of Konjic, there was an ABiH attack against the HVO, and conflict engulfed the entire area of the Konjic municipality. And then there was a minor incident that occurred in the territory of Vakuf. It was soon placed under control. It didn't spread. And then, thirdly, there was a conflict between the HVO and the ABiH which occurred on the Zenica-Vitez axis. That would be number 3. So that conflict was the conflict that is considered to be an initial conflict in Central Bosnia. So those were the events in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In military terms -- well, I can see "Vitez," and you say that there was a conflict in Vitez. When I have a look at the map, the Zenica area and the part below it, below Novi Travnik, would you say that the ABiH wanted territorial continuity which would establish a new pocket, a Busovaca-Travnik pocket? In military terms, was that the strategic objective that the ABiH was pursuing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the strategic objective. The entire area of the Lasva Valley, the Lepenica Valley, or the territory from Travnik to Kiseljak and Kresevo, was to be split into a number of small entities. They were to be separated from each other [marks]. The HVO was to be reduced to minor forces, unable to help each other, and then gradually, one by one, the HVO was to be defeated, the population was to be expelled, and in this way a larger area would have been created for the ABiH or, rather, Bosniak area -- a so-called Bosniak area would be created. That is what happened when Travnik was taken. The HVO no longer had a presence there. They were only in Vitez and Busovaca and in this enclave here. So it was a real military objective. They were thinking, in military terms, separate them, reduce them to a number of small entities, and then gradually, one by one, liquidate them, or, rather, take over -- take the troops, or arrest the troops, or expel them. And when you expel them, expel the population together with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll give the document an IC number, since the witness has marked some numbers there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked portion of document 4D00561 shall be given Exhibit IC01182. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D83 is the following document I would like to have a look at. It's dated the 15th of April. It's from the ABiH. Esad Ramic is reporting to the 4th Corps. It's a combat report. We'll see it up on the screen, and it is important for perhaps an understanding of the ultimatum. I said "perhaps." I'm not certain of anything. So we have a document of the ABiH in which, as you can see, at the very beginning they say that in the early morning the Herceg Stjepan Brigade had attacked the ABiH at Klis. According to this document, it is you who attacked. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic obviously forgot about the 13th and not the 14th. He also forgot about reports in the media that we had attacked them first, for them not to attack us. This is a trick that occurred also on the 30th of June, when Pasalic said, They attacked us, and then we responded and took everything around Bijelo Polje. The Herceg Stjepan Brigade, Your Honours, which has no contact with other HVO forces and was in an -- absolutely incapable of undertaking [realtime transcript read in error "understanding"] any military action in the municipality of Konjic because the balance of forces was absolutely unfavorable for the HVO, and they couldn't attack anyone, because in five or ten days they would have been liquidated and disarmed. Esad Ramic explained this to his commander, who knows what happened. They attacked us, and then we responded and disarmed them one by one, village by village, until 50 villages were disarmed and the HVO had disappeared from the territory of the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to make a correction in line 8. Instead of "understanding," the word should be "undertaking."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, if I understand you correctly, there's an error in this document, and that is that it wasn't the 14th of April, as indicated, but the 13th of April. This document was drafted on the 15th of April, as we can see, and will be registered on the 17th of April in the 4th Corps. So you appear to be saying that Mr. Ramic is presenting a military version which is not totally correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Ramic -- or maybe we don't have the document. What happened on the 13th of April is not described here, because he begins with the 15th of April, and he says that, On the 14th of April, in the morning hours, we had captured the village of Buscak, but, in fact, the ABiH had attacked that village on the 13th. Now, whether there is a report dated prior to this, we haven't managed to find it. There must be one, because these are daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see the next document, which has the same date, 4D453. I'm waiting for it to appear on the screen. Here we are. It is an HVO document dated the 15th of April, because it was received at 12.38 in the headquarters, so one can assume that it is, indeed, from the 15th of April. And it relates to Bradina, Igman, Konjic, et cetera. According to you, what does this document indicate?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document by a brigade commander says that Konjic and the rest of Konjic municipality were attacked -- or, rather, the HVO in this area was attacked by units of the ABiH.
