And now if we compare the two, we will see that the reports are for the 15th of April in both cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the 16th of April with the next document. And so thanks to this document, we can follow. It is 4D33, and it is a document of the 4th Corps. It's a document of the 4th Corps drafted by the security chief, Maric, relating to the events of the night between the 15th and 16th of April. And apparently he refers to Sevici [phoen]. In the English version, it says "Sevici." I assume it should be "Sovici." General Petkovic, what is the situation as described by this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me just correct. The place is Sevac Njive on the Dubrava Plateau, and it is 50 or more kilometres, as the crow flies, from Sovici. This is quite a different area, the Dubrava Plateau area. And the Bregava Brigade is there; that is, the 42nd Brigade of Bosnia-Herzegovina, known as the Bregava Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we are 50 kilometres from Sovici. What is the military situation at this stage, as you knew it, because as the document says, there is an action by the HVO, with the assistance of the Croatian Army, it appears. That is what is written here. What would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the reference to the Croatian Army. Could you assist me? In what line is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the second paragraph, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says: "In order to achieve its ultimate aim, that is, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO has engaged all its forces. With the comprehensive assistance from the Croatian Army, they're attempting to achieve their ultimate goal." Now I see it. I don't know what the Croatian Army was doing at the Dubrava Plateau. Obviously, it wasn't present there. The Croatian Army is far further to the south, close to the borders of Croatia, and not at the Dubrava Plateau. And you will see, from these dates on, that it keeps saying "HV-HVO." These were instructions from the ABiH that in every report they have to say "HV-HVO," and even add to that the extreme section of the HVO. So in all these reports, you will see reference to "HV-HVO." At the Dubrava Plateau at this time, there were no Croatian Army units. The Croatian Army was along the border of the Republic of Croatia in the direction of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The next document is of the 17th of April. It is document 4D -- wait a moment. I apologise. 4D599, 599. It's a bit complicated with all these numbers. It is a document of the 4th Corps, and it is again by Mr. Ramic. There it is. You have the document. And from the beginning, it refers to combats against the HVO in the Konjic area. And then he reviews all the positions of the HVO, Stari Grad, Zlatar, Spiljani, Polje Bijela, et cetera. According to you, what does this document mean, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the military perspective, this document says that there are seven locations where the HVO was, were simultaneously attacked by the ABiH, and these are all locations immediately next to the town of Konjic. The old town is a part belonging to Konjic. Zlatar is on a hill above Konjic. Polje Bijela is also in this area. Babin Nos is where the famous check-point was that is mentioned in UNPROFOR. And the village of Radisine is also Konjic municipality, but several kilometres from Konjic in the direction of Jablanica. But all this is Konjic municipality and the urban area, itself, the urban area of Konjic and the surrounding localities. As far as I remember, there's only one that may be seven or eight kilometres further away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at the end of the document, which may be of some interest. Let us look at the end of the document, please, when Mr. Ramic speaks of a Serb and Croat aggression against the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the very end. According to my reading, there were 60 trucks of men, MTS, artillery action from Borak on Muslim villages, and for him there is no doubt there is an open aggression of Serbs and Croats. What is your comment? He even speaks of co-operation between the HVO and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Ramic's position. By this attack against the entire territory of the town of Konjic and its municipality, the HVO had to withdraw to the so-called pocket that we have mentioned, and the only contact that the HVO had were the Serb forces on the front-line up there. And Mr. Ramic, instead of explaining why the Croats were attacked at these locations, he finds the excuse that it is now the Serbs and Croats who are attacking Konjic. Actually, from this day on, not a single Croat or HVO soldier was no longer in Konjic or in these locations. From this day on, the so-called pocket was formed in the municipality of Konjic with about 1500 civilians and about 300 soldiers of the HVO, and nothing more than that. And such a force of 300 men cannot attack anyone. On this day, they were pushed into this pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's see the next document, 4D430. Let me check with the screen. It is a document addressed to the 4th Corps. It is an interim combat report regarding the 17th of April. You have the document in your own language. And according to what I see at the beginning of the paragraph, there was a request by the HVO for subordination to the HVO of an ABiH unit, and if not, they have to surrender their weapons. And this was refused. That is what it says here. What would be your comment, because this affects what we have already heard about the allegation by the Prosecutor that as of the 15th of April, there was an ultimatum. I won't go into the details. You are familiar with them as well as I am. So this document could go in that direction. What would you say to it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this Colonel Beglerovic is. And that a battalion from Dreznica is supposed to subordinate itself to the HVO, I don't know anything about that, when four or five days before that you saw that Witness Peric said that there was a joint contact on the Bijela Bridge between the 2nd Brigade and the Dreznica Battalion, so I don't know what this is about. I don't even know who this colonel is, obviously from the ABiH, that he apparently attended a meeting in Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have anyone's order, or Lasic's order, or anyone else's order to do anything. I don't know what this is about between these two units. I just know that contact was established between them three or four days prior to this date, on the 12th or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to conclude, from what you have said, that you are denying emphatically that there was a request for subordination from the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. That's not what he said at all. He said he doesn't know anything about it. I don't think that's -- I think that's a completely incorrect mis-characterisation of the testimony. He said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when I ask you a question, after 30 years of professional experience, I think over what I'm saying. My question was the following, and I'll repeat it: In view of the reply that you gave, should one conclude from it that you are denying that there was a request for subordination of an ABiH unit to the HVO? That is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am denying that, and I'm rejecting such a possibility. Colonel Beglerovic apparently is walking freely in Bijelo Polje, without any fear, and I don't see why the HVO would ask Dreznica to give them weapons. This did not happen in the territory of Mostar and the entire Mostar region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I see a document and I read a sentence. I then ask you whether you agree with what the document states. You say, No, and then I try to understand what your final position is. And you have just explained your final position very clearly. This colonel would move around freely, in your opinion, and the issue of subordination of an ABiH unit was never raised, it was never an issue. That's your position. Perhaps it's true, perhaps it isn't. When deliberating, we'll examine this document, together with other documents, and the Judges will then draw a conclusion. But for the moment, I just take note of your position. I don't have a point of view with regard to it. It is your position, and you have expressed it under oath. 4D34 is the next document I would like to have a look at. I'm looking at the document, dated the 18th of April. It's on the screen, dated the 18th of April. The 42nd Mountain Brigade, the ABiH. So it's the other side. Suggestions are made. It appears there are certain security measures that are being proposed, and so on and so forth. It says that co-operation should be established with the Dubrava and Stolac inhabitants, and this should be done through the civilian authorities. As this is a document that emanates from your own Defence, this document, in your opinion, has what sort of objective? What is the purpose of this document, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was written by the head of security, and it's up to him to see what should be done. He makes his proposals to the commander. The object of this document is to establish full contact between communications and issuing of assignments to Muslim soldiers in the HVO, the population in the broader area of the Dubrava Plateau. So this whole system, Muslim soldiers in the HVO and civilians, should be tied up into one single system, and the Bregava Brigade would head that system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I to take it that, according to what you say, this document has its -- wants the ABiH -- or says that the ABiH wants the HVO to be included in certain activities, and this document proves that this is the case, apparently; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document says that the BH Army organs should contact the Muslims in the Croatian Defence Council, and establish full co-operation with them, and agree at what point in time, if that point arrives, they should cross over and join the BH Army. That's the purpose of this. Negotiations with the Muslims in the HVO. They're telling them, Stay there, but when we're ready, you cross over to the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another document, the 18th of April. 4D35 is the number of the document, and it is a document from Pizovic, the 42nd Mountain Brigade. It's a three-page document. This document, it seems, has to do with the situation -- relates to the situation. There's combat, ongoing combat. There's some very precise items in the document. In your opinion, what does this document prove? What does it prove?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, in the Dubrava Plateau area within the frameworks of the 42nd Brigade, emanates from an order by the 4th Corps commander. I don't have it in front of me now. But he issued orders to the entire corps, and, among others, to brigades in Konjic municipality. And the commander of the 42nd Brigade knows what is happening in Konjic municipality, what activities are being launched by the BH Army, and he raises combat readiness for his own unit, probably expecting to be given an assignment from the corps commander for him to try to act militarily vis-à-vis the HVO units. And that is why he undertakes certain steps, when we read about the 2nd Battalion and the 3rd Battalion and so on, to extend his forces along the Dubrava Plateau, thereby creating initial positions which will prove advantageous to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a look at the following document. The same date is concerned, and it yet again emanates from Pizovic. 4D473 is the number of the document. It is addressed to the commander of the Knez Domagoj Brigade. I re-read this document this morning in order to prepare for the questions I was going to put to you. I've been preparing for this for about two years. However, this morning I re-read the document again, and when I did that, I had the impression that Mr. Pizovic was telling the HVO that he wanted to co-operate, that it wasn't a matter of encroaching on zones of responsibility, and so on and so forth. It says that the ABiH had no ill intentions, that there were many Muslim soldiers who were part of the HVO. So how would you interpret this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is a reflection of the situation in which the Bregava Brigade and the 1st Brigade are trying to explain -- the 1st Brigade to explain to the Bregava Brigade, Yes, you can move around the Dubrava Plateau, but you must announce your movements beforehand so that we know where you're going and why you're going; nothing more than that. Now, Mr. Pizovic is replying and saying that he doesn't have any special intentions, and he feels quite strong here. He feels he was given a zone from -- or by Mico Lasic, which he was holding, but that he felt the need to move around. And nobody is questioning that need of his to move around, but it is a military rule, Your Honour, that you can't go into another brigade's area without announcing your arrival. If you announce your arrival, you're free to move around. But Mr. Pizovic is not doing that. He's moving around as he sees fit. But if you read documents from the security organs, Mr. Pizovic, in actual fact, is abusing that and is coming into contact with the HVO soldiers, Muslim HVO soldiers, and he is also coming into contact with the population as well and preparing them. And at the end of this document, Mr. Pizovic says to Colonel Obradovic, Now for you to come to Gubavica, you're going to have to announce your arrival, when you intend to come and when you intend to arrive. So there Mr. Pizovic is saying to Mr. Obradovic, If you want to come to Gubavica, you have to give me prior notice, telling me of your arrival. So it's just a question of having both brigades respect the regime in the area of another's brigade, that they should announce what they intend to do and that then there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The 22nd of April is the same date. 4D90 is the number, a report from Mr. Ramic. We've already seen this in other documents, and it's addressed to the commander of the 4th Corps. I'll check to see that you all have this document. You now have it in the B/C/S version, and the English version will be appearing on the screen. So there is a summary of the situation. It speaks about the liberation of the village of Radesine. There are other locations mentioned, Turije, Zabrdje, and so on and so forth. In your opinion, what does this document mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the continuation of attack by the BH Army against the HVO, and an attack on Croatian settlements in Konjic municipality. We showed you the document in this courtroom, and it was the -- and it concerned 24 villages which the BH Army had taken control of. Mention is made here of those three villages, Turije, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, and that they should not be taken control of until the village of Radesine has been liberated, which is seven or eight kilometres away from Konjic. So they wanted to take control of Radesine first, and then they would go back to Turije, Zabrdje and Zaslivlje, because apart from these three villages, looking at this date, there was no Croatian village in the vicinity of the town of Konjic which the BH Army had not already taken control of. All that remained was these three villages and the village of Radesine. All the other villages were too close to Kostajnica. But around the town of Konjic, itself, these were the three remaining villages, including Radesine, and Radesine would be done with within a day or two, and then Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje would never fall into the hands of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, have a look at the last paragraph. In technical terms, I have the impression that the ABiH was in a position to intercept conversations of the Serbian forces. Is that true? Was it true, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the BH Army was equipped with devices enabling it to tap in to the Serbs and the HVO, and anybody else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you, the HVO, were you in a position to listen to the ABiH and the VRS, to intercept their conversations?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we were also able to intercept them, just as they intercepted us. Well, we had the same devices, the same equipment, both the BH Army and the HVO. The Serbs had stronger equipment than we did. And part of those communications, at a tactical level, was something that we were able to intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I think that when you say "intercept conversations," that that's too broad. Which conversations can be tapped into and which can't? Because this way it appears that we knew too much about them and they knew too much about us. There was several types of communication and conversations, and I'm sure General Petkovic knows what could be done and what could not be done, what could be intercepted and what couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, following General Praljak's technical intervention, when you listened to the ABiH and the VRS, what were you doing, exactly? How were you doing this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we intercepted only radio communication. And in military terms, this is called "the tactical depth," which means not further than seven or eight kilometres in depth. Our equipment was not able to intercept conversations further away. So you had this device that chooses its frequencies. When it comes across a certain frequency, it taps in to that conversation. If it's interesting, it listens to the conversation to the end, then records it, and then processes it further. So the tactical level. We intercepted for as much as the tactical level was concerned, which was seven to eight kilometres in depth, not further than that. We weren't able to tap in to conversations further than that. Those were the devices we had that could be used for that depth. For other depths, you would use other devices, or telephone communication devices, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were able to engage in tactical interception of conversations. Let's have a look at document 4D1344. It's the 8th of May. The date is the 8th of May. As you know, that's the day prior to the 9th of May. It's a document signed by Mladic and Halilovic, and it confirms the desire to re-establish peace. And as of noon on the 9th of May, there's to be a cease-fire. All of this was done in the presence of General Morillon. You, the HVO, were not associated in this matter -- involved in the matter. How do you interpret this document? Is there a link that can be made between the ABiH attack that you supported on the 9th of May in Mostar -- is there a link or not, or is it just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I learned about this document on the 11th of May, when I went to talk to Halilovic and General Morillon in Kiseljak. Before the beginning of our meeting, General Morillon started first and said that two days previously an agreement had been reached between Mladic and Halilovic, with his presence -- in his presence, and that they dealt with problems with forces in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that I knew -- or, rather, they told me that an agreement had been reached then between Mladic and Halilovic. I was just angry when I told Halilovic -- I told Halilovic, when he interrupted our stay in Jablanica and Konjic on the 5th, in the evening, he said he had other things to attend to, he could have freely -- frankly told me that he had negotiations with Mladic. But on the 11th of May, they told me quite openly, General Morillon and Halilovic, that is, that this meeting had taken place because of the problems, as they said, between the two armies in eastern -- the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that I had been completely informed of their meeting and that they discussed matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as for the 9th of May, I don't want to speculate or make any conclusions. I learnt about it three days later, three days after the agreement, that they had met and signed the agreement. Nobody hid it from me. And that was the practice, for General Morillon to ask for meetings, both bilateral and tripartite ones, depending on the problem that had to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say that you learned about this on the 11th of May, but the agreement took place on the 8th of May. At no point in time did General Morillon phone you and tell you, General Petkovic, there's going to be an agreement on a cease-fire between Mladic and Halilovic; we're putting this into place, and it will take place on the 9th of May -- it will come into force on the 9th of May, at noon, and I encourage you to reach the same agreement with Halilovic and Mladic? Didn't he phone you to tell you something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he didn't, he didn't phone me. But before the talks between myself and Halilovic, he said, quite frankly, Halilovic and Mladic reached an agreement in my presence. Now, after this agreement, on the 12th, I and Halilovic reached an agreement, and then General Morillon said, Now it would be a good idea if I had a third agreement. And on the 16th of May, he convened a meeting. And we did, in fact, meet, Mladic and I, and signed the agreement, so that at that moment from the 8th to the 16th of May, he had three bilateral agreements signed, because that's what his position was, and we complied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you participated in all those meetings that were held in Geneva. Wouldn't it have been more interesting -- I don't know, it's just a hypothesis I am putting forth. Wouldn't it have been more interesting for there to have been an agreement between Halilovic, Mladic and Petkovic, between these three signatories? Wouldn't that have been better?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly it would have been better. However, General Morillon at that moment felt that it would be better, in view of the overall situation -- and the HVO could not influence the events in Eastern Bosnia towards the border with Serbia. That's where there were only the Bosnian Serb forces and the BH Army forces - although it does say in the agreement that there would be a cease-fire throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, anyway, General Morillon, in talking to them, in consulting them, he wanted to try and calm the situation down, and that is why he convened this bilateral meeting, just as he accepted to chair the meeting between myself and Halilovic on the 11th. And we signed the agreement on the 12th of May and didn't consider it necessary to include Mladic in that. But subsequently he asked, when we already had two agreements in the bag, that we could have a third. And I flew to Sarajevo in his helicopter for the meeting with Mladic, and I've already told you the outcome of that. So he didn't hide this from any of the three of us. He wanted to have an agreement with all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The following document we've already seen, 4D457. 4D457. There's Mr. Izetbegovic's signature, which you can recognise. It emanates from the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document says that ABiH units are in conflict with HVO units, and they must respect a cease-fire on the 10th of May, 1993, at 1800 hours. So you are referred to in the document, because you have been ordered to immediately meet Halilovic in order to establish the details of this order and how it should be implemented, and also in order to return the relationship between the units of the ABiH and the HVO to normal. So in your opinion, what is the meaning of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document which came into being after the 19th of May, on the basis of talks held at about 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening on the 9th of May between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban, when they agreed that on the 10th of May, they would issue a command -- that each of them would issue a command -- one was in Sarajevo and one was in Grude, so they couldn't have issued a joint command. But the next one is an order from Boban which is identical to this particular order, because we spent three hours harmonising and dovetailing it to make it as similar as possible, both from Mr. Izetbegovic and from Mr. Boban. And it demands that conflicts in Mostar cease, that there should be a cease-fire in Mostar. And let me also add that on the basis of this, that meeting of mine on the 11th of May, which started in Kiseljak, continued on the 12th of May in Medjugorje and went on for three or four days with Halilovic in the Mostar and Medjugorje area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document is under seal. I don't know why. 4D -- it shouldn't be broadcast to the outside. 4D00456. The same date, the 10th of May. It's from Mate Boban. And as you have just said, the two documents are almost identical if you compare them. What does this document state, General Petkovic? In your opinion, why is this document of interest?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, it's the same document as Mr. Izetbegovic's document, that is to say, for conflicts to cease between the BH Army and the HVO in Mostar, and that I and Halilovic should meet and draw up an agreement to fully bring about a cease-fire and to resolve the situation. Now, this document, if you're interested, let me tell you that I and Mr. Boban were in Grude. We were on the phone with Mr. Izetbegovic, and we started with point 1 and then dovetailed it, fine-tuned it; point 1, item 1, item 2, item 3, and so on. And if you look at the two documents, they're almost identical. The heading is a little different, because we introduced the agreement reached in Zagreb on the 25th of April. But, anyway, this document is the result of a three-hour telephone conversation, because one man was in Sarajevo, the other was in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, is there a reason for which this document was drafted one second before 1800 hours, because you can see the hour is 1759 hours. Is that quite accidental, or was there a desire to issue this document just a second before 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, this document was completed sometime around 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. This was obviously faxed to someone, and then this is the date when it was faxed. Now, I took part in the compiling of this document, and I had communication with Sarajevo, and I know that by 2.00 in the afternoon the two copies had been dovetailed and fine-tuned, and then it was processed further. So at this time, the 10th of May, somebody sent the document to someone at 1759, so it doesn't matter -- there's no significance in this one-second difference between 1800 hours and 1759.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see now document 4D00307. It's a document by you, and it is 10 days later, that is, the 20th of May, 1993. And it is addressed to General Wahlgren and General Morillon, and it regards the Medjugorje Agreement and its implementation. Why did you send this document to Zagreb and to Morillon?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the agreement and Boban's order, and my agreement with Halilovic, General Wahlgren, who was the commander of all the forces for the former Yugoslavia, and therefore General Morillon's superior, he joined in at this stage, and he wanted General Morillon and UNPROFOR to assist as much as possible. And that is why I felt it necessary to inform General Wahlgren, who had got involved in the events in this area and who had an interest in dealing with the situation as soon as possible, and of course to General Morillon, as he was a co-signatory of the joint document. And I'm saying here what the HVO had done. I said that it had released all the civilians in the barracks. I didn't say "all captured civilians," but "all civilians." And I indicate everything else that the HVO has done. And I draw your attention to the last part of this. It says that the forces of the ABiH have still not withdrawn from the Konjic sector, so UNPROFOR cannot patrol the Vrci village, Seonica-Podhum road, as envisaged by the agreement, because the UNPROFOR said that the same day it entered Mostar, it would enter the Konjic area as well, and they were not able to enter, as we see on the 20th of May. And my request is if General Morillon could do something along those lines in agreement with the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall pass on to document 948, which may clear up some events connected to the 30th of June. 4D948. This is a document by you; hence, the interest of this document. It's an order addressed to the South-East Operational Zone of Herzegovina, as you can see. And the preamble indicates that the situation is such that there is a Muslim aggression, and their efforts are to control and occupy the Neretva Valley. And that is why you issue an order indicating a series of measures. And in point 2, you say that you need to regroup forces in Bijelo Polje to prevent Muslim forces from attacking. In military terms, how is one to understand this document.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, this document was drafted after intensive combat for Travnik had already been conducted and after the HVO was practically facing defeat in Travnik. This document was then drafted because the HVO was about to be defeated in Konjic, too, and throughout that area. This was also done after it came to light that the ABiH was sending some of its forces in the direction Mostar and as far as Dreznica. At that time, there was no fighting that would be of concern in Bijelo Polje, Mostar, and in that area. But I believed that those Muslim forces might at one point in time have been in a position of attacking the HVO, so I warned the commander of the operative zone in South-Eastern Herzegovina that he should find a way -- if we [as interpreted] attacked from the axis of Jablanica-Bijelo Polje-Mostar, he should find a way to have forces that could deal with it. So it was a warning -- an order in which a warning was given. But at that point in time, there was no fighting in the area. It was just an order, the purpose of which was to warn, given the situation that prevailed a little further to the north of Bijelo Polje and further to the north from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I think there's a critical error in the transcript. In line 22 on page 67, it says here that General Petkovic said "if we attack from the axis Jablanica-Bijelo Polje-Mostar." He said "if we were to be attacked from the axis Jablanica-Bijelo Polje-Mostar," rather than the HVO attacking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite correct, Your Honour. I said if the army were to attack HVO units in the area of Bijelo Polje, but from the direction of Jablanica-Dreznica towards Bijelo Polje. Of course, I asked the 3rd Brigade also to be on the alert, and also to the 2nd Brigade. But I am saying, once again, there's no fighting at this point in time in Bijelo Polje or Mostar. This is a warning order, in view of what was happening to the north of this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You anticipated the question that I was going to put to you, but it should be in the transcript. In this order, there is mention of raising the level of combat; that is, to prepare for a potential event. And I see, in point 8, when you are asking for the fortification of lines, et cetera, so this document is not an attack document. Is it mobilising everyone? "In the event that ...," is that how we should read this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Resources are being mobilised, in the event they are attacked, and that is why it says that some other positions in depth should be prepared, that is, 300 or 400 metres behind, and, Should you be pushed back from that position, you continue the struggle from the next position, which is a normal military procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when there is an order for an attack, in the order must there be mention of the time of the attack? Should there also be an indication of a system of communication? Should there also be other technical instructions so that one can consider such an order to be an order for an attack?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. In an order for an attack, you have to indicate the exact date of the attack, the time of the attack, when you will launch it, will it be 4.00 a.m. or 5.00 a.m., and you must also envisage the dynamics of the attack, how it will evolve. And also in the assault units, the assault units have to be brought there at least 24 hours before the attack, that is, close to the line from which you will attack, and they must be on full combat alert, because it doesn't mean that if you say that you're going to launch the attack at 4.00 a.m., that you may not change your mind and say you will start it earlier. But you have to give the date, the time, also the time when the artillery will provide support by firing at the front end, also the direction of the attack, the dynamics of the attack, and the ultimate target of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should one also envisage a reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, Your Honours. You don't launch an attack only with the front-line forces. There's the first echelon, then the second echelon, and then there are also forces protecting the wings, and there are also forces that may be infiltrated behind enemy lines to disorganise him so that the front can -- front-lines can more successfully carry out their task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break: In such an order, should not one also envisage the weapons, a medical corps, food; should not all these things be mentioned in the order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, such an order is comprehensive. First, you indicate information about the enemy, his deployment. Then you give assignments to your own forces. Then, thirdly, the decision, what it is you wish to achieve. And, fourthly, then you give assignments to each of your units. And then after, if you have tank support, you give tasks to the artillery, what its role is, when it will start to provide support. It must have its own plan of action. I'm surprised you didn't ask me any question about the Toplica diaries. Then regarding the engineers, the communications, the logistics, the medical corps, security, et cetera. An order has more than 20 points covering everything. I hope that in the cross-examination of my counsel, we will show such an order, and then we shall see. Therefore, an order on an attack has a large number of points, and it must cover everything, in terms of time and space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. I have focused on a few principal points. I could add also: Should there be a code-name? But I didn't enter into the very minute technical details. Anyway, after the break we'll look at document 4D702. And before the end of the day, that will be my last question, I will have a dozen or so documents, depending on the speed of your answers. So we'll meet again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. A small correction of date. As this morning we received planning for the Coric Defence, Mr. Andabak will come from the 8th to the 11th of March. Therefore, the oral decision that we rendered this morning should take into account these dates, that is, the 8th to the 11th of March. General Petkovic, 4D702. It's not on the screen yet. Here it is. It's a document that you sent on the 30th of June - this is an important date - to Mr. Wahlgren and Morillon, and you refer to the issue of Muslims. What I am interested in is on page 2 of the English version, where it appears that according to what you say, you informed General Morillon, on the 26th of June already, of the possibility that the Muslims may organise an attack -- an assault on the town of Mostar. Do you see that? The 26th of June, you told him this orally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. On the 26th of June, 1993, General Morillon arrived in Medjugorje, and he called us to come and discuss certain issues with him. And I, among others, warned General Morillon of the possible danger in Mostar, in view of all the events taking place in Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina. This is a period when Travnik had fully fallen, as had Kakanj, on the 26th of June, except for a small area in Klis, Turije, and Zabrdje. We didn't have our forces at all in the territory of Konjic municipality, and the forces of the ABiH were approaching Mostar gradually. I warned him of this danger, and suggesting that a meeting could be organised with Halilovic, or for him simply to warn them of this, to bear this in mind. This was on the 26th of June, when he visited Medjugorje. And we had quite a lengthy conversation at the time. And then I wrote a letter to Mr. Wahlgren as well, counting on him to talk to Mr. Izetbegovic and others, if possible, to prevent an attack by the ABiH on Mostar and the areas around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I take note to what you have said. Therefore, this letter that you sent on the 30th of June, was its aim to explain to the international community what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, Your Honour. This was sent to them for them to learn about the situation. And also on the 15th of June, when we signed the tripartite agreement, we took upon ourselves the obligation that, through our officer -- liaison officer, we would immediately inform the operative headquarters of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak on anything happening by the opposing side. This was a major move by the ABiH, and I personally wrote this letter to General Wahlgren and to General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the time. We have another 45 minutes. Let us look at all the remaining maps. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I have a small question on this letter. You write about the, I quote, "so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH)." Why do you say "so-called"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Trechsel, after everything that had happened, I asked myself, Is that, indeed, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or is it not, and whether I belonged to such an army or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, 4D502 [as interpreted]. It is a map that you headed "The situation in June 1993," and it is going to appear on the screen. Here it is. Could you, in brief and in military terms, describe the situation, because you were the one who prepared this map.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. With this map, I wanted to show all the things that were happening in June 1993. So let me start with the beginning of June, Travnik, and part of the municipality of Novi Travnik. The ABiH attacked units of the HVO, and by the 12th of June, the ABiH fully controlled Travnik. Thousands of Croats were expelled. Kakanj, the red line is missing around Kakanj, which is meant to indicate that on the 15th of June, Kakanj also fell; that is, the ABiH took control of Kakanj, and 10.000 to 12.000 Croats were expelled and sought refuge in the municipality of Vares. Similarly, in June the ABiH attacked Vakuf. In June, also, there were the first attacks by the ABiH on Fojnica, but they didn't succeed in gaining control of Fojnica. And June was one of the worst months for all the other Croatian enclaves in Bosnia and Herzegovina, starting with Kiseljak, where symbolically I have these two circles, Kresevo, Busovaca, Vitez, this whole series of markings for fierce fighting. June was one of the most difficult months for the HVO in Central Bosnia. I think that was the final decision of the leadership of the ABiH and Mr. Izetbegovic to settle accounts with the HVO in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just correct the transcript. At page 73, line 10, this exhibit is given as "4D502," and it is 4D561 -- I'm told 562. I did have in mind it was 561, but there were probably two versions of it, then. It's 562, apparently, is the actual one up on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to say that this means that Travnik, where there were HVO units and ABiH units, shows that Travnik was in the hands of the ABiH at the time, and there were no longer any Croats in the territory of the municipality of Travnik. This also concerns parts of the municipality of Novi Travnik, which is near the line with the Army of Republika Srpska. The Croats were expelled from that area. The ABiH took control of Travnik, of part of Novi Travnik municipality, and they took full control of the Kakanj area too. So this is how I would depict it, symbolically. Our enclave, our HVO enclave, moved in this direction [marks], and this is the enclave -- they didn't take Fojnica at the time, so it was -- the HVO was still present there in June. And Konjic can't even be seen here, apart from a small part in Klis. We've seen that, but Konjic isn't here. These were the first attacks on Vakuf, and it was a preparation for a subsequent attack in July that was launched against Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked portion of document 4D00562 shall be given Exhibit IC01183. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will move on to the Mostar map before the 30th of June. 4D621. We have the map there. General Petkovic, we have Mostar here. Could you comment on the map that you have, that you, yourself, made?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was prior to the 30th of June. It's the situation when the HVO and the ABiH were together at a joint line facing the VRS, and that line extended, well, from the 4th Battalion -- from their 4th Battalion - I'll draw it here below this point [marks] - the 2nd HVO Brigade is defending this line [indicates], they continue to Mostar, above Mostar. The 1st Brigade of the ABiH comes to the line with its three battalions. Then the HVO 3rd Brigade is at the line facing the Serbs here [indicates], and then we reach Blagaj. There's an independent battalion of the ABiH here. It's called Sargan, and they continue to hold the line facing the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS. That is the joint line that we held before the 30th of June together with the ABiH. The HVO and the ABiH held that line. If you take this red line here [marks], you could say it's the line of the VRS. I will mark it in this way so that you can see that it is the line of the VRS [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the Registrar to provide a number for the document, and then I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked version of document 4D00621 shall be given Exhibit IC01184. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you said that there was the 1st ABiH Brigade, the 2nd HVO Brigade, the 3rd HVO Brigade deployed at certain positions, et cetera. What I would like to know is: at the time could a Muslim or Croat civilian move around freely from the north to the south, and in the opposite direction too? Could they do this in the areas that we can see in green and in blue?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, green -- the green colour and the blue are symbolical. You're supposed to be able to see the entire area. The army was at the lines that I have already shown. The army wasn't in the depth. Everyone who needed to move from Mostar towards Bijelo Polje and further on could do so, or from Mostar to the south in the direction of Blagaj. They could also move in that direction. It was a joint line, the forces were joint forces, and I see no reason for this not to be possible. Similarly, the HVO could freely enter the barracks, the Northern Camp that is here where I have stated that it's the 1st Brigade. They could enter that area. They could go over Tito's Bridge and enter the Northern Camp. It wasn't a problem. So if it was necessary for someone to go in one direction or another in this area, it was possible for that person to do so quite freely. If the authorities allowed this, organised groups of people could move around. Otherwise, that wouldn't be the case. I mean the authorities in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and be concise, because I have other maps and I would like to conclude. 4D622 is the following map. It's the situation in Mostar after the 30th of June, 1992. Could you comment on this map, since we can see the markings "VRS," "ABiH," "HVO"? What does this map mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the previous map, this map means that between Eastern Mostar, Bijelo Polje, Dreznica, and Jablanica, there are no HVO units. That entire area is now under the control of members of the ABiH. The HVO has been driven out to the western bank of the Neretva River. The VRS remained at the positions that it had previously occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that one should conclude that the HVO had been driven back and that the ABiH had control over the entire area depicted in green. My question: Could a civilian from East Mostar go to the north or to the south through territory that was under ABiH control?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge Antonetti. A civilian could move through that territory, because in that territory there was no longer an HVO presence. No one was there, apart from the ABiH. The ABiH regulated movement and decided how many people could pass through that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll move on to the map on Mostar, Jablanica and Konjic. It's 4D1216. We'll see it in a minute. It depicts the situation up until the 30th of June, and then there's the situation on the 30th of June. There it is, we have the map. Could you comment on this map, which, according to you, depicts the situation in the area prior to the 30th of June, or up until the 30th, of June, as you like?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions of the VRS is identical to the positions it had a few months earlier. These are the positions occupied by the VRS. If you start from the south, this line here [indicates] is a line that was under the control of an ABiH battalion, it faced the Serbs. This blue line here [indicates] was held by the 3rd Brigade of the HVO. I don't know why this pencil -- this pen isn't working. This is the line that was held by the 1st Mostar Brigade. Could you please provide --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the pen doesn't work, we can't see what he is showing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that it will work now. I'll try to sign -- no, it's not working. It's probably all right now. It's not working, but I can explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps the map could be put on the ELMO, and another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could place it on the ELMO. Wait, I'll give you my map. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I'll mark the Serbian line first, the line held by the Serbs [marks]. These are the positions of the VRS, as I have already said. They didn't change for a very long time, and they held these positions here. Now I will mark the positions and the lines under the control of HVO units [marks]. So this double line represents the line occupied by the HVO units, the 2nd Brigade of the HVO. And now I'll show the position of the 3rd Brigade [marks]. To the north, near Konjic, there's a small enclave. I'd like to correct this, because a witness quite rightly observed something. This enclave borders on these positions here [marks], borders on the village of Prevlje, borders on the position of the VRS. So this shows the situation correctly now. Together with the HVO, lines were held by members of the ABiH in areas where their units had been deployed. So I want to show you that situation too. This the Blagaj area [marks]. This is the Mostar area, it's the slopes above Mostar, which is where the 1st Brigade was located together with its three battalions [marks]. This part here was under the control of the 4th Battalion of the 1st Mostar Brigade. We also called it the Dreznica Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say that, as has often happened in the past, at the moment we're not getting, as we go along, any clear link between the transcript and the map that we're going to be able to follow in the future, because the words "here" and "there" are perfectly comprehensible right now, as we're watching Mr. Petkovic do it, but they won't be when we're later looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll mark this again once I've completed the line [marks]. This area that I have just marked was under the control of units the Municipality Defence Staff of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mark it with a letter or a number, that will help us find the place in the transcript that is concerned, the relevant place in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll start from the south. Number 1 is Blagaj [marks], the battalion of the ABiH in Blagaj. Number 2 [marks], in the area of Mostar, the line towards the Serbs is held by the 1st Mostar Brigade. Number 3 [marks], the front-line towards the Serbs, is held by the 4th Battalion of the 1st Mostar Brigade, or the Dreznica Battalion. Number 4 [marks] is being held by the Municipal Defence Staff of Jablanica of the ABiH. And number 5 [marks], I've put number 5 in two places. That is the front towards the Serbs held by the 7th Brigade of the ABiH. So all the numbers I have indicated refer to the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is the joint front-line held up until the 30th of June by members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council in the area north of Konjic, across the territory of Jablanica municipality and the territory of Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you sign the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, take the map, please, and give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked version of document 4D01216 shall be given Exhibit IC01185. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next map that will be placed under the ELMO is 4D1207 -- 1217, I'm sorry. And using the ELMO, we'll be saving some time. So we're still in the same geographic area on the 30th of June. Could you explain the situation exactly as it was on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, Your Honours, after the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina captured HVO positions north of Mostar and certain positions south of Mostar, the situation was as follows: The Army of Republika Srpska held the same positions [marks]. I have marked in red the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska. I shall now mark the positions towards the Serbs held by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina [marks]. This line tells us that facing the Army of Republika Srpska, after the 30th of June, in the area from Konjic, across Jablanica municipality, up to Mostar, Eastern Mostar, and Blagaj, there are no units of the HVO; that is, HVO units in this area have no contact with the Army of Republika Srpska, and they organised a new front-line on the west bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you sign the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a number for this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This colour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Petkovic, just a question of detail. In an earlier map -- can you take the ELMO -- the map a bit down on the ELMO? No, that's up. Down, yes. The enclave of the HVO shown north of the white spot, you have indicated that there was a mistake, because it was actually up to the line of the Serbs. Would that still be true? So I think it would be correct if you also put in this correction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you [marks]. Let me just strengthen the red line to mark it more visible [marks]. Thank you for your indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked portion of document 4D01217 shall be given Exhibit IC01186. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There are two other maps, the situation in July 1993. Under the ELMO, please. The document -- I don't have the number now. 4D -- I can't remember the number. 563, 563. 4D563, yes. General Petkovic, will you please comment on this map showing the situation in July?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can. [Marks]. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in June, captured Travnik. And in July, the HVO did not return to Travnik, so the HVO has been expelled, the military as well as the civilians, and it is in the hands of the ABiH. [Marks]. The same applies to the municipality of Kakanj. I will sign as soon as I explain. Kakanj and the municipality of Fojnica are fully under the control of the ABiH. And the little blue enclaves that remain, I can mark them with numbers, if you wish. They are the remaining Croat enclaves. And I forgot to add that Konjic, too, with the exception of a very small area which I will mark in blue [marks], is all that remains of the Croatian enclave, just symbolically. So you see it is next to Konjic. This is the situation as it was in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please sign, and we will have a number.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. But I wish to point out that 90 per cent of Bugojno had already fell. But if necessary, we can mark that on the next map, because on the 2nd of August Bugojno was left without any Croats. They were expelled.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked portion of document 4D00563 shall be given Exhibit IC01187. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have September, and then we also have November, and that will be the end of it. Yes, the number is 564, 4D564.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the situation was as follows at the time indicated [marks]. I have marked all the places in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina from which, militarily, the HVO was defeated and the Croat inhabitants expelled from these areas. But in the area of Konjic, I have to put a little dot to indicate an enclave [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just marked by the witness, which is 4D00564, shall be given Exhibit IC01188. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last map, it is 4D567.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on this map we have a presentation of everything. I have nothing to add. All the places have been crossed out, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik, part of Zenica, Vares, Fojnica, Konjic, other places from which the Croats were expelled and no HVO forces are there. The HVO has been defeated by the ABiH. And the little dot remains in Konjic. And we see the number of inhabitants who were in those places, but were expelled by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the situation in November [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the general tell us which inhabitants he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat inhabitants, Croat inhabitants who were expelled from all these places here, and that is the situation in November 1993. These two enclaves in Central Bosnia remain as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The numbers appearing on the map are numbers indicating the Croats who were expelled from the areas. For example, for Travnik, according to you, there were 25.000; Vares, 9.000; et cetera. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Those are roughly accurate data. They are not smaller than this. There may be more. I don't know how many Croats from other areas may have come to Vares and were then expelled. The Croats from Kakanj were no longer in Vares. They went further on and they disappeared from this area. Konjic had about as many Croats who came from other areas, but they left the whole region. They were expelled from this region. So UNPROFOR says that the Croats left, and for the Bosnians, they say that they were expelled. Then there were local Croats plus those who came from Serb-controlled areas. There were 25.000 in Travnik, and now there's not a single one left. Unfortunately, even now there are none, with the exception of a few hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4D00567 just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC01189. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very small question, and you don't need the map. Mr. Petkovic, how did these figures come about? Are these your estimates, are they in some other official document? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Judge Trechsel, these documents and these figures were kept in our Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, and an analytical team attached to Mr. Boban's office monitored the expulsion of Croats and kept records on the total number of Croats expelled, those who had lived there, those who had earlier on fled from the Serbs and settled there, and then they were expelled together with the locals from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, thank you for having answered my questions. I intended to use two days. Unfortunately, it has extended to three days. There were rulings to be handed down, objections, and so on, so I was a bit longer than I had planned. Thank you for answering my questions. I asked you about your positions, specifying things with the help of some documents on some occasions. That is what I wanted to tell you. Before closing, a small precision regarding Witness Miroslav Desnica, who will be testifying on the 8th of March, 2010, and not on the 2nd of March. Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On the last break, a few of us heard for the party. Since we are, for obvious and understandable reason, are not invited, others who have spent the last four years are, allow me to convey on this, the only way, our best wishes for your 80th birthday, which was actually yesterday, as I heard. So happy birthday, Mr. Prandler, and take care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm very much in a situation that it is difficult for me to answer to you, besides thanking you for your very kind words. I am really sorry that you are not invited, but it is the rules of the game, and I cannot alter those rules, of course. But I wish everyone here in the courtroom all the best, and thanking them for their co-operation and their spirit of friendly relations, if at all it exists in a courtroom. So thank you, and I really thank, actually, Mr. Prlic for his nice words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have something quite different to raise. It will be probably my turn tomorrow, so I appeal that in view of the hundreds of millions of dollars that are being spent, and that a pen isn't working, and when a film is being shown, it will and will not, and then we give in and you give in, so if we had acted in this way in wartime conditions, there would have been an additional 100.000 dead. Yesterday, I mentioned the word "professionalism," which means, (a), to know your job, and, two, to do it honestly for the salary you receive, so let them act in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, make sure that tomorrow that the pen is working. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for standing at the last moment. But we tried to deal with it directly in communication with the Detention Unit by e-mail, but we received no reply. So if you could ask from the Registry to make it possible, when the accused return to the Detention Unit, for General Praljak to take two bulbs, because he needs those bulbs to be able to read the documents overnight. We brought those electric bulbs. The guards said we could, and now, according to the Rules, we cannot send them to him. So could the Registrar intervene so that we give those electric bulbs to General Praljak. Of course, the guards would assist us here, but the guards in the Detention Unit do not allow it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Registrar please forward this request so that I don't have to go and buy some bulbs myself. It will be done, Mr. Registrar. Tomorrow, we will have the cross-examination by the other Defence counsel. I wish you all a good evening, good afternoon, and we meet again tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
